title: What is the difference between String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer, and when should each be used (single-threaded vs thread-safe)?
shortTitle: What is the difference between String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer?

s1_definition.profdef: `String` is an immutable sequence of characters; every modifying operation produces a new String, so it is safe to share but inefficient for repeated edits. `StringBuilder` is a mutable, growable character buffer that supports in-place append and insert without creating new objects, and it is not synchronized, making it the fast choice for building strings in a single thread. `StringBuffer` is the older mutable buffer with the same API as StringBuilder but with every method synchronized, making it thread-safe at the cost of some performance. The rule of thumb is: use String for fixed text and sharing, use StringBuilder for building strings in single-threaded code, and use StringBuffer only when multiple threads must mutate the same buffer.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a String is like a printed certificate that can never be edited; to change it you print a new one. A StringBuilder is like a personal notepad that one clerk uses to draft a statement, writing and erasing freely and quickly because only that one clerk touches it. A StringBuffer is like a shared logbook at the counter that several clerks might write in at once, so it has a lock-and-key so only one clerk writes at a time, which is safe but a little slower. You pick the certificate for fixed records, the personal notepad for solo drafting, and the locked shared logbook only when several clerks really share one buffer.
s1_definition.oneliner: String is immutable, StringBuilder is mutable and fast for single threads, StringBuffer is mutable and synchronized for multiple threads.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `String` is an immutable sequence of characters; every modifying operation produces a new String, so it is safe to share but inefficient for repeated edits. `StringBuilder` is a mutable, growable character buffer that supports in-place append and insert without creating new objects, and it is not synchronized, making it the fast choice for building strings in a single thread. `StringBuffer` is the older mutable buffer with the same API as StringBuilder but with every method synchronized, making it thread-safe at the cost of some performance. The rule of thumb is: use String for fixed text and sharing, use StringBuilder for building strings in single-threaded code, and use StringBuffer only when multiple threads must mutate the same buffer.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a String is like a printed certificate that can never be edited; to change it you print a new one. A StringBuilder is like a personal notepad that one clerk uses to draft a statement, writing and erasing freely and quickly because only that one clerk touches it. A StringBuffer is like a shared logbook at the counter that several clerks might write in at once, so it has a lock-and-key so only one clerk writes at a time, which is safe but a little slower. You pick the certificate for fixed records, the personal notepad for solo drafting, and the locked shared logbook only when several clerks really share one buffer.

**One line to remember:** String is immutable, StringBuilder is mutable and fast for single threads, StringBuffer is mutable and synchronized for multiple threads.

sections.s2_technical:
String is immutable. Its characters live in a private final array, and every operation like concat or replace returns a new String. This makes String ideal for fixed values, map keys, and safe sharing across threads, but repeatedly editing a String, especially in a loop, is expensive because each edit allocates a new object.

StringBuilder is a mutable buffer backed by a growable char or byte array with a count of how many characters are used. Methods like append, insert, delete, and reverse modify the buffer in place. When the buffer fills, it grows, typically doubling, which makes a series of appends amortized linear time. StringBuilder is not synchronized, so it has no locking overhead and is the fastest option, but it is not safe to share across threads without external coordination. It is the default choice for building strings within one thread, such as assembling a statement or a log message.

StringBuffer predates StringBuilder and has an almost identical API, but every public method is synchronized on the buffer instance. This makes a single method call atomic and thread-safe, so multiple threads can call append on the same StringBuffer without corrupting it. The cost is synchronization overhead on every call, even when only one thread uses it, which is why StringBuilder was introduced in Java 5 as the unsynchronized, faster alternative for the common single-threaded case.

A senior nuance is that StringBuffer's per-method synchronization does not make a sequence of operations atomic as a whole; if you need a compound operation to be atomic, you still need external synchronization, so in practice sharing a mutable buffer across threads is often better handled by giving each thread its own StringBuilder and combining results. Another nuance is capacity management: both builders let you set an initial capacity to avoid array resizes, which matters for large outputs, and both are far better than String concatenation in loops. In modern code, StringBuilder is used almost everywhere, String for fixed text, and StringBuffer is comparatively rare, reserved for genuine shared-buffer scenarios.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank builds each customer's statement in a single thread and needs it fast. This is exactly where StringBuilder fits — mutable and unsynchronized.

Problem 2 — A shared audit log buffer is written by several worker threads at once, and it must not get corrupted. This is exactly where StringBuffer fits — synchronized mutation.

Problem 3 — The account number and fixed labels never change and are shared widely. This is exactly where String fits — immutable and safe to share.

The code has a `StatementBuilder` using StringBuilder, an `AuditBuffer` using StringBuffer written by multiple threads, and a `BuilderChoiceDemo` main class that exercises both.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the fixed account id SAV2001, a 5-line statement built in one thread, and 4 threads each appending 100 audit entries to one shared buffer.

Step 1: The account id SAV2001 is a String, immutable and safe to share. It is used as a fixed label throughout without any copying concerns.

Step 2: The StatementBuilder creates one StringBuilder with an initial capacity and appends the header and each line in place. Because it is single-threaded, no synchronization is needed, so building is fast.

Step 3: A single toString produces the finished statement string, which is then logged.

Step 4: The AuditBuffer wraps a StringBuffer. Four worker threads start, each appending 100 entries concurrently to the same buffer.

Step 5: Because StringBuffer synchronizes each append, the concurrent writes do not corrupt the buffer; every entry is recorded intact. If a StringBuilder had been used here without external locking, entries could interleave and corrupt the buffer or lose data.

Step 6: After all threads finish, the buffer reports exactly 400 lines, confirming no corruption, which demonstrates StringBuffer's thread-safety contrasted with StringBuilder's single-threaded speed.

```text
INFO: Statement:
National Bank of India - Statement for SAV2001
Line 0: TXN amount 100
Line 1: TXN amount 100
Line 2: TXN amount 100
Line 3: TXN amount 100
Line 4: TXN amount 100
INFO: Audit lines recorded (no corruption) = 400
```

```text
  ─── Single thread: StringBuilder ───
  StatementBuilder → sb.append()×N (in place, no lock) → toString() → statement

  ─── Many threads: StringBuffer ───
  worker0 ─┐
  worker1 ─┼─ audit.record() → buffer.append() [SYNCHRONIZED] → no corruption
  worker2 ─┤
  worker3 ─┘
            ▼
  buffer = 400 lines intact
  (StringBuilder here without locks → interleaved/corrupted)
```

```text
  ┌────────────┐          ┌──────────────────┐
  │ Statement  │ 1 thread │ StringBuilder     │  fast, no lock
  │ Service    │────────→ │ (per request)     │
  └────────────┘          └──────────────────┘

  ┌────────────┐  N threads ┌──────────────────┐

```

```text
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Type           mutable  synchronized  use case  │
  │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────│
  │ String         NO       n/a           fixed text, keys, sharing │

  Senior caveat:

    For compound atomicity, add external synchronization, or give

```
sections.s6_takeaway:
String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer differ along two axes: whether they are mutable, and whether they are thread-safe. String is immutable, so every modifying operation produces a new object. That makes it perfect for fixed values, map keys, and safe sharing across threads, but it is inefficient for repeated edits because each edit allocates a new object.

StringBuilder is a mutable, growable character buffer. Methods like append and insert modify it in place, and when the buffer fills it grows, so a series of appends is amortized linear time. It is not synchronized, so it has no locking overhead and is the fastest option, which makes it the default choice for building strings within a single thread, like assembling a statement or a log message. The trade-off is that it is not safe to share across threads without external coordination.

StringBuffer is the older sibling with essentially the same API, but every method is synchronized on the buffer. That makes each individual call atomic and thread-safe, so multiple threads can append to the same StringBuffer without corrupting it. The cost is synchronization overhead on every call, even when only one thread uses it, which is exactly why StringBuilder was introduced as the unsynchronized faster version for the common single-threaded case.

So my decision rule is straightforward. I use String for fixed text and sharing, StringBuilder for building strings in single-threaded code, which is almost everywhere, and StringBuffer only when several threads genuinely must mutate one shared buffer. In our banking code, account numbers and labels are Strings, each customer's statement is built with a StringBuilder in one request thread, and a shared audit buffer written by several worker threads at once uses a StringBuffer so the concurrent appends stay intact.

The senior point I always add is that StringBuffer only makes each single call atomic, not a sequence of calls, so if I need a compound operation to be atomic I still need external synchronization. In practice I often prefer to give each thread its own StringBuilder and merge the results at the end, which avoids contention entirely and is usually both simpler and faster than sharing one synchronized buffer.

---

keyPoints: String: immutable — every modification creates a new object
StringBuilder: mutable, NOT thread-safe — fast for single-thread use
StringBuffer: mutable, synchronized (thread-safe) — slower due to locking
Use StringBuilder by default, StringBuffer only when shared across threads
